utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Since no preliminaries were announced, we'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution is going to start with 65 ter 13835A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we resume, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We were just waiting for one second while a document comes up. Sir, thank you for your patience yesterday. As you saw, we had some technical difficulties. I want to return now to a few documents that I wasn't able to get to yesterday. Before you is a 21 August 1992 report from prison warden Branko Vlaco of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca. The report states: "Pursuant to the request of the Rajlovac Brigade, for the purpose of performing physical labour, 29 prisoners were taken out for labour." Is it correct that the Rajlovac Brigade made requests to this prison for prisoners to perform physical labour?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't know about this. All I know is that there were works at Zuc, combat was ongoing, and the line was being fortified. This was the link between the Vogosca and Rajlovac Brigade. This is from the prison so I really cannot -- I don't know if it was these people who were holding the line up there who came to take these people. Perhaps it was at their request, but I don't think that the request was sent from the command. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, who would have the authority to make it a request?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. These were the guys who were on the line. It could have been an oral request for people to come and help. Those people who were at the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you were the deputy commander of the brigade at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And it seems from your answers that you do have some possible knowledge of this. Is it correct that you were aware that individuals were being brought to the front lines to perform physical labour?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this did happen but I don't know about this situation. I mean, I know that they would go and that they would be kept there so I assume that that would be that position for them to go to help, so I cannot say that this did not happen. Yes, these things did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, your previous answer was therefore half of the truth and not the whole truth when you said, "I don't know about this. I don't know about this." You know that prisoners were taken from the prison and were escorted to the front line where they had to do labour, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an occurrence, that's why I'm saying I don't know about this particular case, but there were cases of people being brought to the front line for purposes of fortification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you know of these incidents, perhaps not specifically this one. Who asked for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the units would ask for it. I mean all the units. I cannot say this one did and this one did not. It was known that the units were doing that, the people who were at the positions because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who sent the request to the prison? Or was it just everyone on the lower level going to the prison and say, Give me 20, 25, 30 people, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and how did you come to know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because it was a usual occurrence. I don't know if it was a written request or, as we say, I need people to dig five shelters or five trenches for fortifications and then perhaps they would also request a digger machine to work on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was usual occurrence. So do I have to understand that knowing that this was usually done, that you agreed that even with this procedure of asking at the lowest level would be acceptable for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, there was no way to prevent that. There was no way to prevent that because then you would go into a conflict with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. I didn't ask you whether there was a way to prevent it. I asked you whether you apparently agreed this to happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not agree. I personally did not agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you do to express your disagreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there. I didn't give approval. I didn't submit such requests. I mean, I did not have any influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. I asked you what you did to express your disagreement as the deputy brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know what to say. All I know is that I was not in favour of that, of people from the prison being taken. I wasn't even in favour of those people being held in prison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I knew that there were prisoners there, I didn't know who they were, what they were, or where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that they were taken to the front lines to do labour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that they were going but I didn't know who the people were at the front lines, where they were. I cannot know that. Here in this case, these people were at Zuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you know that these people were at Zuc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the document, from this document I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do you see it in the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says at the bottom. I mean, it says that they were returned to the prison, 29 of them, that somebody was asking. I don't know if they were where they were, how many days they were there, but it does say who returned them so we would need to see in which zone they were, whether they were in the area of the Vogosca or the Rajlovac Brigade. Here, it says at the request of the Rajlovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you started saying that you don't know anything about this specific event. Later, you said I know that they were at Zuc, which you had mentioned before as well. And then asked you: "How do you know?" You said, "I see it in the document." But the document not in any way refers to Zuc. That is, these are inconsistent answers and I'll invite Mr. Weber to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P6750 [Realtime transcript read in error "P6760"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6760 is admitted into -- I'm sorry, I made a mistake. I was waiting for the transcript. P67 and then you said 60?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 50. I apologise. 6750 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P03194 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated three days later, the 24th of August, 1992. It is a Rajlovac Brigade request to hand over prisoners from Operative Group Vogosca. The document is from brigade commander Lieutenant-Colonel Golijanin. The request states: "We hereby request that you hand over to us 10 prisoners from your prison, in order to help us in digging trenches at Zuc on 25 and 26 August 1992." Sir, is it correct that actually these requests were made from the brigade command for these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this one or the previous one. The previous one, they probably worked the first day near the Vogosca Brigade where Major Mitrovic was and then to come to us to work. And then we made the request, so I can see my signature so that means that I signed it. Mitrovic was at the position there. Probably in relation to this previous one, we also made a request. I don't know how many we requested. That's why I'm saying that this previous one was at Zuc and then this is a continuation, meaning that that combat line was being fortified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In your answer, you just said: "The previous one, they probably worked the first day near the Vogosca Brigade where Major Mitrovic was." Sir, in the previous document that we looked at, there was no reference to Major Mitrovic. How is it that you know the previous one related to Major Mitrovic who we now see on the document from three days later?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if Major Mitrovic was then there. It says which ones they took and which ones they returned. If he went to the prison, he must have gone in an official capacity from the command. And probably you had the lower organs making the request, and you see in the previous document who the people were who returned the prisoners. And you can see in the previous document that there is no Mitrovic and there was no request. You can see that it says based on an oral request by whoever it was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat the last portion of your answer. You were saying that -- you were referring to the previous document, "there is no Mitrovic and there was no request." Could you please repeat what you said after that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This request, most probably when they were there, it's possible that they were there from the Rajlovac Brigade. I mean, possibly. I cannot be sure. But it's possible because that's where they linked up. And so then to continue the line, the request was made. So they assumed that since they were already there, they were not being taken back, so the assumption was that they should just continue to fortify the lines. And I think Mr. Jovo Mitrovic died at those lines in the line of defence. What was expected was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to pause here, there's no need to repeat yourself. Who is Major Jovo Mitrovic? What is his position in the Rajlovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo Mitrovic was a reserve major. His wife was killed. He found himself there. He wasn't in the barracks. He would come to the barracks and he held positions, I mean above Dvorovi, where Zuc and Zabrdje connect. I mean, he was in that area. I mean, he had a sort of unit of his and he was, I mean, trying to set up these positions and to link that up with Rajlovci, down with the barracks. I mean, I mean that was the area, I mean, where there were no houses, and that was the area that was being defended. He was a reserve officer. He came to the TO. He reported and he was carrying out, I mean, assignments that were needed to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Was he battalion commander, was he a platoon commander, a company commander? What was his command level?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was a platoon commander or a battalion commander in any case his task was to unify everybody in that area, the troops, the works. He was the most senior officer. I think he was over 55 years old, 55, 56 years old at the time, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to look at one more document on this topic. I don't know if Your Honours had any more questions on this specific one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for the witness. First of all, did I hear you say, or at least that's how it was interpreted, that you saw your signature on the document shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, then, I'll take you back to one of your previous answers when you said that you didn't know about the other incident. "All I know is that there were works at Zuc, combat was ongoing, and the line was being fortified. This was the link between the Vogosca and the Rajlovac Brigade. This is from the prison so I really cannot -- I don't know if it was these people who were holding the line up there who came to take these people. Perhaps it was at their request, but I don't think that the request was sent from the command. I don't think so." That was your answer in which you clearly suggested, and I sought verification of that in one of my follow-up questions, you clearly are suggesting that such requests were not channeled through the command. Five minutes later you tell us that you signed a request for prisoners to be sent. That is inconsistent and untruthful in one way or another. Any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This first request, that was the connection as I said, that was the connection. I don't know about the first one. Well, like this, this is a few days later. It means that there was a need, a need for that to be fortified so that that was done, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the details. I'm asking about an answer which clearly suggests that such requests were made from the lower level and not channeled through the command, whereas, at least on this one document, you tell us that it is your own signature which was put by you on a request for a similar situation. I'm asking you about this, not about whether it was on Wednesday or Tuesday or whether the one followed the other. You gave an impression which is contradicted by the document just shown to you and signed by you. Any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the first position and that's all right here. Again, I note, I apologise to you, I note this was, I mean, that they asked most probably and then they asked for more without the command, I mean, without the command so for something to happen. I mean, I mean, then the command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. You're not responding to my question. I'll read another part of your testimony to you. You were asked: "Who would have the authority to make a request?" Your answer: "I don't know. I don't know. These were the guys who were on the line. It could have been an oral request for people to come and help. Those people who were at the positions." You're clearly denying the involvement of the command, whereas from the document, it can be seen not only that the command was involved, but also that you had personal knowledge about this. This is not the whole truth you're telling us. Any further comment on my point, not on your points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you have just said, that it was possible to get the soldiers from the prison without the command, means that they wouldn't have addressed the command in the first place. It means that there was no -- there was a need for work so they were with you for two, three, five days, it doesn't matter. They didn't finish. And then the command would get involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I established that you're not -- that you're not responding to my question. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to 65 ter 13834.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you will be a 2 September 1992 report, again from Mr. Vlaco, the prison warden in Vogosca. In this report, we see that 21 prisoners were taken to perform physical work at Zuc. Were you aware of this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that these prisoners were regularly -- actually, you've already answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6751, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to change topics now. Is it correct that you previously testified about the mopping up of Sokolje in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a document on the screen, I gave -- I gave -- I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through some materials, but before doing so, just so we have a little orientation here. Sokolje is a village to the north of Sarajevo near Visoko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Where is it within -- in the north of Sarajevo? Where would you place it near?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokolje is opposite the Rajlovac barracks. There's the railroad, there's the road, and then there's the village of Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please again have P353. This time we're going to go to page 368 of both versions, the original and the translation. If I could please have 368 in the original notebook, the J series. Not the B/C/S transcription but the original B/C/S notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, before you again is one of General Mladic's notebooks. This is an entry from 26 July 1992 concerning a conversation he had with Captain First-Class Nedjo Lemez. Captain Lemez was a member of the Rajlovac Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lemez, I don't know about him. I don't know about Major Lemez.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like to direct your attention to the bottom of the page, and I'll be reading on to the next page, concerning what appears to be a proposal by General Mladic. The entry states: "I propose the following: One, for the Rajlovac Brigade to prepare in about 5 days in the general area where it," and if we could continue the next page, "where it has about 2.500 men and to liberate Sokolje." I'll just stop there. Were you aware that General Mladic proposed the liberation of Sokolje?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that General Mladic proposed that but I just know that there was a lot of pressure coming from the civilian organs in Rajlovac to liberate Sokolje, especially the Serb houses. As for people who fled to Rajlovac from Sokolje, I know about that pressure. Pressure, I felt it, others felt it, and that's why I clashed the most with all of these people from the municipality of Rajlovac because I was against that kind of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that your superiors in the military were in favour of attacking Sokolje?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it correct? I don't know. I don't know if it's correct. Possibly there's an order, I know this was done. I know it was not good. What happened is what I assumed. That's what I'm telling you now. That's what I assumed and that's what happened. It was impossible to carry out that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll go through some more things but here we see -- just coming back to something I discussed with you at the very outset of my examination. We see in this entry that it appears the Rajlovac Brigade now has in July 1992, at the end of the month, about 2.500 men. So I put it to you that you've not provided an accurate account of how many men were in the Rajlovac Brigade. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have a comment. There were never 2.500, that's not possible. There weren't more than 500 people in Rajlovac, in that brigade. It couldn't have been more than 500. However, if people came from elsewhere, later on there was assistance from other units and they came from the Krajina front line, over here, in this area, so it couldn't have been 2.500. It couldn't have been more than 500 that were made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, but just for the record, our position is that that's not a truthful answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So could the Prosecution now please have 65 ter 31264, page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to your Karadzic testimony related to Sokolje quickly and I'd like to go through quickly what Judge Kwon asked you about this. I'll read it to you since it's not translated before you. During your Karadzic testimony, Judge Kwon asked you: "What I'm interested in is the statement that you obstructed many in action, for example, the mopping up of Sokolje and Brijesce hill. Is that true?" You answered: "Ye. Well, yes. I was not inclined to be going towards those people. This is something that would have required a lot of casualties of innocent people. When you go somewhere, it means the civilians and the soldiers would become casualties and the effect would be not much. So there was practically no need. There was practically no justification for such an action for this act." Do you stand by this testimony here today in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I understand from your previous answer that the military advantage sought by mopping up Sokolje and Brijesce hill was not justified because the risk of civilian casualties was too great?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Risk for civilians, for soldiers, and for taking up these positions in that area. Even if all of it were to be done without casualties, that situation could not be maintained up there, at those positions, with the personnel that the Rajlovac Brigade had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to your view on this, did you inform your superiors of it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I did not. I didn't have an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31260 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this, Mr. Weber, you did put to the witness that Captain First-Class Lemez was a member of the Rajlovac Brigade. The witness was unable to confirm this. Now, the document you've shown him on e-court page 367, it says: "Conversation with Captain First-Class Nedjo Lemez." And the first entry reads: "Commander of Rosulje [phoen] Battalion in the Ilidza Brigade." Any reason why you put to the witness that it was the Rajlovac Brigade where the document says, at least suggests, that it was the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My apologies. I had two Lemezes and two excerpts I was using, and the other excerpt that I was going to be using had that individual as a member of the Rajlovac Brigade. Thank you for catching that, Your Honour. I was wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this context, you were wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah, I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a 19 October 1992 order from General Galic related to the final combat activities in several areas including Sokolje and Brijesce. According to item 3 of this order, the commanders of the Rajlovac, Ilijas, Vogosca, and Igman Brigades were all involved with this operation. Is it correct that at this time, you were actually in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th, yes, I was in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When General Galic issued this order, is it your evidence that you did not voice your objections to these operations? Is that how we should understand your answer, your previous answers?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I'm saying about before when I was in Rajlovac, I did not have the opportunity to object. Now this is coordinated action, that is to say, the organisation of higher units for carrying out a mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you express any of your concerns to General Galic at this time in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that General Galic was aware of the entire situation throughout the area. He had intelligence organs. Now whether he asked me personally and whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Could you please answer the question whether you expressed your concerns to General Galic, not what General Galic knew already but whether you expressed your concerns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not at that moment express my concern because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6752, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6752 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And one last document. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31238 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 30 November 1992 order to attack from the Rajlovac Brigade which there's later indication that it was approved by General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution stay on this page of the B/C/S original and go to page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item 2, enumerating the task of the brigade, the order states: "Our brigade has been instructed to launch an attack from its starting positions to the right of Lemezovo Brdo-Zabrdje-Smiljevici toward Svabino Brdo and Brijesko Brdo, cut off the village, surround the enemy forces in the village of Sokolje, thoroughly mop up the villages of Sokolje, Brijesce, and Brijesko Brdo," and it continues. In November, did you articulate any concerns to General Galic when he was -- or when the brigade, Rajlovac Brigade was being tasked with mopping up Sokolje and Brijesko?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I did not because the -- our command was already involved in different tasks, and as chief of engineering, I did not have the opportunity to make suggestions. I was not an operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Could the Prosecution please tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6753, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the Prosecution's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few, Your Honour. Could we please have in e-court document 1D04082. I think that its P number -- I mean, I think that this document has received a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly, I didn't manage to write it down yesterday when the Prosecutor was cross-examining but it is on our list and that's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge Moloto is correct, I did not tender it because Mr. Stojanovic had indicated that he was going to be tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So there is no P number yet, and I take it, then, that you will tender it at the end of the questions. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vujasin, just a few questions. Please focus on this document that is before you now. Yesterday, it was shown to you. According to military rules on the basis of which the VRS acted, who appoints a brigade commander, which organ?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their superior command, one step above.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, would that be the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the general staff, one level above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When looking at this document, could it have been correct from a formal point of view that you would be appointed brigade commander in this way?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes; practically, no. So formally, yes; legally, no. The most senior officer who happened to be there, yes, according to our rules. It's only for a particular task for a particular amount of time, a limited period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a permanent decision from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska that you would act as brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please restart your answer, whether you ever received a permanent position from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska that you would act as brigade commander. Could you restart your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive that from the General Staff, no order like that except for this, what is here, Vukota Vukovic, I said a moment ago legally yes, legally no -- I mean, no, operatively, yes. But the first decision was received by General Milos Golijanin, who was a lieutenant-colonel at the time. He came from the General Staff and he came to the command in Rajlovac and he took over the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at document P6746.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you now tendering this document, 1D4082?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I certainly plan on having this document admitted. I would just like to recall that it is on the list that I provided yesterday before we started. It's one of those nine documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that is a list of documents you intend to tender as associated exhibits and as you know, it always has been the preference the Chamber that the number of associated exhibits would be as low as possible and that the parties are encouraged to introduce any documents through a witness. So therefore, since you're doing that, it seems that it would be appropriate not to leave it on the list of associated exhibits but rather to tender it now, if that's what you wish to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, then I would like to tender document 1D04082.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D642 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, what you have before you is the document that was shown to you by my colleague, the Prosecutor, and you spoke about this document. This is what I'm interested in, could you please explain the following to us: 40 105-millimetre shells are requested but it's for the needs of the Rajlovac Brigade and it's requested by the commander of the operations group. Does this indicate the question that you had, whose artillery was this that would use these shells?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations group consisted of the Rajlovac, Kosevo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters did not hear the third brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already explained this. So where there is artillery, I mean then -- then their targets would be engaged so this indicates the use of that and they would have powers over the use. I mean the operative group, yes, the operations group. Or whether they would go to another place, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the brigades which were forming the operations group? You mentioned the Rajlovac Brigade, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Kosevo Brigade, Kosevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we now have all three. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please look at document P353, page 368, could we have that in e-court. That is General Mladic's notebook, the one that we looked at a moment ago. Before that, for the sake of context, could the witness please take a look at the previous page, 367. Could we please take a look at that first. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, in order to have the context, this is a note concerning a conversation that General Mladic is having with Captain First-Class Nedjo Lemez on the 26th of July, 1992, as General Mladic says here, and then there are these footnotes concerning what this is all about and what it was that they had been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now, can we take a look at the next page in both the B/C/S and the English versions. This is what it says on the next page, after all of these statements that were made by Nedjo Lemez and that are written down there: "I propose the following ..." and then the text says number one -- Could we now move on to the next page. It continues that there's a big power struggle going on. It is difficult to deal with a -- no, can I read this right? I think it's Unkovic. And also they need assistance in terms of weapons, ammunition, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question, the commander of the Main Staff, can he make proposals to someone or is his decision only and exclusively in the form of an order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think on the basis of the briefing that the commander of the Main Staff hears, now what can he do in that position? This is something that the people who attended the meeting should think about. That is my understanding. Now what he would do if he were in the place of those people who came to brief him. Now that's what I have to say. Otherwise, the commander issues orders, so there's no discussion about that. That is not debatable. The commander said what he would do and that means that he is giving guidelines to these people, how they should be thinking, how they should be preparing units for these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When it says that in the broader area there are 2.500 men, the area of defence of the brigade, can that be a narrower area or a wider area or a clearly defined area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm missing -- Mr. Stojanovic said "in the broader area." I don't see reference to a broader area, I just see a reference to the Rajlovac Brigade has about 2.500 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it speaks about the general area. That is perhaps in -- that's the translation on page 368, last line. And if there's any need to verify that, whether it's broader or general, then we could do that, but please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is my question: What is written here is: "In the broader area, there are about 2.500 men." Now, can a brigade have in its defence area a broader area, a narrower area or a clearly defined area?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brigade as a brigade has to have its area of responsibility. That is a certain area that is given to it according to certain rules. It is a certain area. Now, it depends on the situation, attack, defence, or whether it was singled out and whether it can go to other areas, whether it received a task like that, so a certain area is clearly defined with boundaries. And there are certain points. It says what it is on the left and what it is on the right, and where they meet up with others and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any general idea about how many inhabitants there were in the area of defence of the Rajlovac Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the exact number. I cannot say that. I didn't even know what the municipal boundaries were at the time, but I don't believe there was more than 500 soldiers. If there were perhaps 5.000 troops and citizens altogether in the entire area, that would include the police, the work-duty force, the president of the municipality, then you would need a maximum of 10 per cent of able-bodied men to defend that area. Then if you add any other settlements to the brigade, if you expand the zone, then there is a possibility that you would go for a higher number. In this case, it happened in the summer that there was an order from the corps command delineating the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that came in June or July, so then one part facing Ilidza became part of the Rajlovac Brigade area. So I'm saying that this is why perhaps there is a larger number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get some assistance, please, Mr. Stojanovic. You've been talking about the broader area. I don't seem to see that on the translation. Are you able to help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it's page 368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What I see on the screen is 367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see "general areas," I don't know whether the original says "broader area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That matter has to some extent been addressed and the parties will look at whether there's any translation issue there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, did you at any point in time while you were on duty in the Rajlovac Brigade receive any order from a superior command to expel or transfer the civilian population from Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received any order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. How much time would you still need so as to know whether it makes sense to conclude and then take a break or whether we should take a break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just need to cover one topic very briefly and I don't think that it would take longer than a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break a little bit later than usual. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to end with questions relating to your assessment, Mr. Vujasin, of the severity or the difficulties of the action in Sokolje. You had the opportunity to comment on that today. Was Sokolje a dominant feature in relation to your unit's position and was that a place from where your unit had material and human losses on a continual basis?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a slope and it was a more favourable position in relation to Rajlovac. There are all these features, Zabrdje, Brijesce, it's more dominant than all these features and then it runs on towards Orlic. It was dominant in relation to Zuc as well. So in that whole area of responsibility, the brigade was not in a favourable position. I note that there were daily instances of people being wounded or killed. Allegedly a civilian came and he was moving towards the command and he was killed right in the middle of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. A question: Units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that sector of Sokolje, were they deployed in civilian facilities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian facilities were used. There were no military facilities there in that area from before. There were no military facilities there from before so civilian features were used and strengthened. Trenches, roads. They were fortified. They were taken up and primarily used for trenches. The houses of Serb families were used for that, and all these families came to the barracks in Rajlovac and they were the ones who initiated that these houses be liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. We will finish. Did I understand you correctly that a part of Sokolje was inhabited by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you understood me correctly. And you can see on the maps that all these are names of people who were in Rajlovac, I mean, in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujasin. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, any more questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber has no questions either for you, Mr. Vujasin, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzino, I assume. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make the solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Dzino, you will first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You will find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for the -- for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to slowly speak your correct first and last name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Stojan Dzino.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, at one point in time did you provide a statement, a written statement to the Defence of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we look at document 65 ter 1D03961 in e-court, please. And could we look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Stojan, I want to ask you if the signature on the page that you see in front of you is yours and is the date written on the page written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I ask you about the truthfulness of this statement, would you be kind enough to tell the Trial Chamber if in preparation for your testimony today, you noted that in paragraph 14 of this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 14, where it says: "From the president of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac," what needs to be deleted is "Serbian" and the rest would remain unchanged?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then paragraph 61 of your statement also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Paragraph 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- contains the words: "In the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac." Again, we would need to delete the word "Serbian" from there.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you also tell me that in paragraph 26 - and I would kindly ask that we look at this paragraph together - instead of the abbreviation "VRS," it should say "TO."

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to cover this in my questions. I would like to indicate that in paragraph 6 of this statement - and this is also something that the Prosecution pointed out in preparation for today's testimony - in the B/C/S version, it states that according to the 1991 census, there were 999, 999 Serbs, whereas in the English version, one 9 is missing. So in the English version, it should also state 999. And thank you for your understanding here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, now that these corrections have been made in the transcript, Mr. Dzino, if I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give the same answers as you did in your written statement now after you have stated the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would now like to read the summary of the statement of Witness Stojan Dzino.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any intention to tender the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I also suggest before I read the summary that the statement be admitted and given a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objection to the tendering of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the statement would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D3961 will be Exhibit D643.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When the war erupted in the municipality of Rajlovac, Witness Stojan Dzino was a member of the TO. Due to troubled interethnic relations, they were guarding their villages. With the forming of the VRS, he became part of the local unit, and then in December 1992, he took over the duties of battalion commander. And then from early 1994, he was appointed assistant commander of the 4th Battalion of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade for morale. In his statement, he speaks about the situation in his area in 1991 and early 1992, about the arming and training of Muslims, and attempts to settle the dispute through negotiations. He asserted that the armed conflict in his area did begin on the 29th of May, 1992, when the Muslim forces used mortars to attack the hill of Krstac, north of the village of Ahatovici. And then during the following days, the conflict spread to Serbian houses in the village of Bojnik, to the barracks in Butile, and then again towards Krstac. With his unit, he personally took part in the fighting when the opposing side was defeated and disarmed. In these battles, there were casualties on both sides and numerous weaponry and military equipment was seized, as well as 19 ABiH soldiers were captured which -- who were then handed over to soldiers from the Rajlovac barracks. They were treated in a humane way. Throughout the entire war, his unit was in defensive positions. They had a numerically superior adversary facing them who in the fighting used 82-millimetre mortars, a tank from Golo Brdo hill, and 105-millimetre howitzers from Hrasnica. They also used civilian facilities for the deployment of troops, weaponry, and equipment. He cites specific facilities where members of the ABiH units were located. There were never any professional snipers in his unit. He will testify about the specific offensives of the ABiH army against the positions of his unit, and he asserts that signed cease-fires were mostly violated by the opposing side. During the war they had substantial losses, i.e., 114 killed, one person missing, and about 600 wounded fighters. Finally, he notes that there was never any oral or written order from higher VRS commands to carry out attacks against civilians in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, could we please look at paragraph 56 of your statement, which now has the number D643. In this paragraph, you say: "As for sniper fire and snipers, I state categorically that in the four years of warfare, I never saw a professional sniper in my unit or other units of the SRK." My question is this: Did your unit have weapons, rifles that could use sniper ammunition and which could be fitted with optical sites or hunting optical sites?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said, "I never saw a professional sniper in my unit." What is a professional sniper to you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: A professional sniper to me is a soldier who completed training as a sniper and it's a soldier who would need to be kitted out with different devices, a suitable rifle, suitable ammunition, protective equipment and everything else. And this is something we did not have. None of our fighters went for that training. And may I expand a little on my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak more slowly and in less detail, please.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Thank you. We did not have any snipers. The best sharpshooters, soldiers, would receive snipers so that in the course of combat they would be able to use them because we did not want to waste any ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, these events that you speak about in your statement, the ones that began as of the 29th of May, and we're talking about the local commune of Toposevici [phoen], where were you at that time when this happened? Where were you living with your family?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I was living in my house in Mihaljevici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask a question before you go to the next topic. Mr. Dzino, did you have non-professional snipers in your unit; in other words, people who were not necessarily trained but who were sniping anyway, using this sniper ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about the beginning of the war, I was the platoon commander and I did not have a single sniper in my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber where was your house and your village of Mihaljevici in relation to the village of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: My house was in a mixed settlement, but specifically my hamlet had the largest part of the population who was Serbs, but there were also Muslims and Croats. The entire local commune had a mixed population but the inner core of the village of Ahatovici was settled exclusively by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These villages, were they adjacent geographically?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: If somebody came from elsewhere, they wouldn't know where one would start and where the other one would end. Literally houses were next door to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Information about the number of persons wounded and killed, this information that you present in your statement, does this pertain to soldiers and civilians or does it pertain only to soldiers who belonged to your unit?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: This pertains only to soldiers who were members of my unit. In addition to that -- I have to give a more extensive answer. I don't know exactly now, but at one point in time, a veteran's organisation was established and I was elected president of this veteran's organisation. That is to say that I have completely documentation about persons who were killed and wounded, so the place where a person was killed or wounded, also a place where somebody was buried and so on and so forth. I think there were 15 casualties among the civilians, I think. And then also there was the war unit Orla that did not make up part of this 114. They are a work organisation and they also had some 10 casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These days when the war just started, were professional soldiers involved or were these simply self-organised locals?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Well, we were organised from the 1st of March, 1992. That's when a member of a Serb wedding party in Sarajevo got killed. That night barricades were put up, and from then onwards, people hardly ever went into town. I just happened to be there. Actually, it's not that I just happened to be there. I was working at the post office, so I went to work and it took me all day to get there because of the barricades. The Serbs organised the defence of their own houses, so it's not that it was weapons or whatever, but some people had hunting guns, others had other things, so we sort of organised ourselves but this was just in front of our own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, just another answer that I'm expecting. In this organisation of yours, were there any professional military men or were these just self-organised locals?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Just self-organised locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally, were you one of these self-organised persons?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you specifically at that time before May and June in Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: We didn't have any positions. We did guard duty at night, and everybody, Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, everybody was involved in agriculture during the day. And during the night, we had these night shifts, guard duty. I have already stated all of that in my statement and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is contained in your statement we don't need to hear about that really. So I won't have any further questions for you so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Stojanovic, was a bit unclear. You should perhaps clarify what do you mean by "in this organisation of yours," as you said, and put to the witness. To understand the context, it would be better to clarify which -- to which organisation you are referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this word "self-organised," that you were self-organised. My question is: What do you mean by that, that you were self-organised?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was. Several families lived there, Serbs, and one family had its organisation, another had its own organisation. At that time, there were no squads, platoons, whatever. People were not armed. But let us say conditionally that these were squads of these families. So then one was my family Dzino and then in this other squad, there was this other family. That's the way it was. That's the way it was organised. But there was no front line. There was no line. During the night, for the sake of the safety and security of their families, people stood guard in front of their houses during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzino.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time I have no further questions for you, so could you please now respond to the questions that will be put to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution and you find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzino.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, by the 26th of May, 1992, you were a platoon commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And your platoon was part of the Rajlovac Brigade. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: It couldn't be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can you explain what unit your platoon was a part of on the 26th of May, 1992, when you were commander of that platoon?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: We are going to be within the Rajlovac Brigade throughout the war but that platoon had just been established. The need was felt to do that because combat activities in the Sarajevo front took place every day. We were supposed to get organised. Now, I didn't know -- I mean now that I'm speaking about that, we were within the Rajlovac Brigade. But once we select this platoon and when the soldiers select me as platoon commander, I did not know then what brigade I belonged to. However, there is no denying that we were members of the Rajlovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mihajlo Vujasin was the first commander of the Rajlovac Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: He certainly was, no denying that. But at that time when I established this platoon, I did not know who was the commander in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in mid-June, he was replaced by Lieutenant-Colonel Milos Golijanin as the commander of the brigade. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Certainly, but I don't know about those dates either, when that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you became a battalion commander in 1992, your battalion was also part of the Rajlovac Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 14 of your statement, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And actually, let's take a look at that, D643, please. Yeah, I see it's on the screen. Could we go to e-court page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, in paragraph 14, you refer to a request made on the 29th of May, 1992, by Hasan Mujkic to Jovo Bozic, the then president of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac. This request was to evacuate the women and children in Ahatovici to Sarajevo. You go on to say an agreement was not reached because the Serbs considered this to be a preparation for an attack on Serbian settlements. You state: "As soon as the women and children are gone, then the men can do as they please, is what we thought." You recall these events, yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, between the 29th of May, 1992, and the 2nd of June, 1992, an attack was launched by Serb forces on Ahatovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: The Serb forces carried out a counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. But regardless of semantics, there was an attack, whether it was an initial attack or a counter-attack, by Serb forces on Ahatovici between the 29th of May and the 2nd of June, 1992. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: That's not correct. If you did not understand me about counter-attack, then this is how I'm going to explain it to you. On the 29th, around 2000 hours, the Muslim forces shelled the Krsnica hill. On the morning of the 30th of May, at 6.50, likewise they shelled the houses of my family. And Luka Damjanovic, Marinko Zdrale, and my daughter-in-law Mila Dzino, they were all wounded so they hid the barn. After that, there was combat. How you are going to characterise is your affair, but we carried out a counter-attack. And the fighting went on until the 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was all admitted by Mr. Jeremy. He said, well, even if would be a counter-attack, it would still be an attack. A counter-attack also is an attack, isn't it? So therefore there was no need to explain as you did because that was all included in Mr. Jeremy's question. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzino, you've referred to mortars being involved in this attack. Now, in paragraph 21 of your statement, you say -- you refer to a number of attacks from Orasnica and from Ahatovici, and I think those might be the events that you have just referred to in your answer. And you say: "The battle was waged with mortars at a distance." So, Mr. Dzino, it's correct, isn't it, that when the Muslims in Ahatovici refused an ultimatum to surrender, their village was shelled; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: No. What you are talking about happened on the 30th, the 30th of May, in the evening. I mean this ultimatum. I found out from people -- I mean, it wasn't a special organisation. All the people who had rifles were there and they said that Hasan asked for the Muslims to go out. So then we understood that this was no command. It's not that an attack was being expected and so on and so forth. So this shelling start on the 30th in the morning at some point, but at any rate after 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. So on the 30th of May, 1992, Ahatovici was shelled. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Not correct. Places from where there was shooting were targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I just try to get back to facts, nothing else. Were any shells, mortar shells, fired at Ahatovici or targets within the Ahatovici area by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzino, your unit was involved in this attack. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: You are trying to say that we attacked something or someone. We were defending our houses. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness, I stop you again. An attack includes a counter-attack. You've told us now two or three times that there was a counter-attack. You told us you told us that mortar shells were fired at positions in Ahatovici. Please, if Mr. Jeremy uses the word "attack," please understand it in that way, that is, counter-attack, whether he agrees or not but he follows your language in this respect. Would you please not again and again respond to matters which you have clarified already where Mr. Jeremy uses language which is in accordance with your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, when Ahatovici was being shelled on the 30th of May, 1992, those women and children who had requested to be evacuated from Ahatovici, they were still present in Ahatovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, by the 2nd of June, 1992, Muslim civilians from Ahatovici surrendered to the Serbian military; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at an exhibit in connection with this, P03793.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzino, on our screens is a report from the Romanija Brcani CSB of the Bosnian Serb MUP on events in the Sarajevo area. If we see at the bottom of the page it is dated the 3rd of June, 1992, and we see it is type signed "Analytical and Information Service." And in paragraph 3 of this document we read: "In the area of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, MZ local commune Dobrosevici, we engaged in fierce fighting with the Green Berets from the village of Ahatovici who, with the support of HOS, Croatian Defence Forces members from Kiseljak attacked the villages of Dobrosevici, Mihaljevici, and Golubici. The enemy was overwhelmed. The village of Ahatovici was liberated and is controlled by the Serbian Army." Mr. Dzino, it is correct by the 3rd of June, 1992, Ahatovici was controlled by the Serbian army; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So is it your position that this report, this MUP report is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Ahatovici came under control on the 4th of June. Because on the 4th of June, in the final fighting, we had one casualty and two Muslim soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. So by the 4th of June, Ahatovici was under control of the Serbian army; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to focus on the final two sentences in the same paragraph that I've been reading from and they read as follows: "Some 50 Green Berets and HOS members were captured and are being interrogated in the Rajlovac barracks." Mr. Dzino, you are aware that men from Ahatovici were detained following the takeover of Ahatovici by the Serbian army. Yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you're also aware that many of those persons were beaten, some of them to death. Yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I don't know. Your Honours, may I put a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You cannot put questions. You were asked whether you were aware of many of those persons had been beaten, some of them to death. And you have answered that question that you're not aware of that. That's an answer to the question, and just wait for the next question to be put to you by Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that you were not aware of it at the time or that you never gained any awareness of beatings and in some cases killings of men who were taken from the village of Ahatovici to the Rajlovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: The first time I came to the Rajlovac barracks on the 28th of June, 1992. And if you are asking me about prisoners of war, my unit killed 13 Muslim soldiers and captured 19. Of those 19, none of them, absolutely not a single one was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said "if you ask me," but that's not what Mr. Jeremy asked you. Mr. Jeremy asked you whether it was only at the time that you were not aware of beatings and people being killed in the barracks or that you never gained any awareness of such events. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] when I came to the barracks, to the unit, and this happened later, I found out that there were such things. But this happened after a month or two. At that point in time, I wasn't even working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you became aware one or two months after such beatings and killings may have happened. Next question, please, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, were you aware that some of those same persons who were taken from Ahatovici were subsequently loaded on to a bus and told that they would be exchanged, and at one point this bus was stopped, Serb forces got out, and the bus was attacked with small arms and rocket launchers. Were you aware of this particular event?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And at any time had you gained any knowledge about this particular event or is this the first time you're hearing of it today?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: It's an ambiguous question. I found out about the events and I'm not hearing of that for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So when was it that you first found out about this attack on the bus?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Was it in 1992, 1993, 1994? Can you give a rough time frame? During the period of the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: During the war, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the early part of the war or at the end of the war, in 1992 or in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Before 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the document that we've been looking at. I'm going to read the next sentence in the same paragraph I've been reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I nevertheless ask you, was it briefly after it had happened, that is, the summer of 1992, or was it considerably later that you learned about that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Significantly later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, so I'm looking again at the document on the screen before us and I'm going to read the last sentence of the third paragraph. It states: "The Serbian army has temporarily sheltered ethnic Muslim women and children in the Gavrilo Princip OS, primary school." Now, Mr. Dzino you were aware that hundreds of civilians from Ahatovici were detained in various locations in Rajlovac; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Well, this is new, the elementary school, the primary school Gavrilo Princip. I didn't know where they were being detained actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. So you knew that they were being detained but you just weren't sure of the exact locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, it's clear from the answers you've provided that on the 4th of June, 1992, the Serb army was in control of Ahatovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Entered Ahatovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on that same day, the 4th of June, 1992, the mosque in Ahatovici was destroyed. Yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at an exhibit in connection with this, it's a picture of the mosque. It's P2510. This is the report of Prosecution expert Andras Riedlmayer. And if we could please go to page 214 in the English and page 215 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Witness, you said that the -- your forces entered Ahatovici on the 4th of June. One of your previous answers was: "Ahatovici came under control on the 4th of June," and then you explained why. So therefore, that's -- saying that it was not under your control but you entered Ahatovici only is inconsistent with one of the previous answers you gave. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzino, just to pick up on the Presiding Judge's question, is it correct that on entering Ahatovici on the 4th of June, 1992, the Serbian army gained control of Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the building on the screen before you as what used to be the Ahatovici mosque?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: I believe that it is but I do not recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you actually saw this being destroyed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it was destroyed by the Serbian army; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: Well, if you wish, I can describe the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: First of all, could you confirm whether or not it was destroyed by the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN DZINO
utterances.text: The mosque was destroyed at the point in time when the Serbian army entered Ahatovici. I was observing that from a point.
